items.reason: The d4 bishop is White's strongest piece, so trading it is a real motive. Nxd4 is still stronger, keeping the g7 bishop.
Rg8 saves the h8 rook and hits the queen; after Qh6 the knight escapes to g3 with tempo.
h6 opens no f8–g7 diagonal and Ng5 isn't pinned; it attacks Ng5 but ignores the e5xf6 threat.
Ne4 does centralize the knight, a valid point. The main idea, trading off Black's bishop pair with Nxf6, goes unmentioned.
Nc6 attacks no white piece, so there is no tempo; it also leaves the pin on f6.
Taking the free queen with the knight is correct, but no bishop check exists here; that claim is false.
g3 is the third rank, and the h4 bishop is itself moving. Bg3 escapes the g5-pawn attack.
There is no rook fork. The real issue is the Bb4 pin on Nc3 and Qd2 along the diagonal to e1.
Nxd5 removes White's outposted d5 knight and regains a pawn via Bxf5; it trades no central pawns.
f8 is Black's back rank, not the second rank, and a knight on f8 cannot guard a8.
King already on g1; Qxg2+ is the capture itself, and g2 is defended by king and Qd2, losing the queen.
Bxe4 takes the e4-knight, not c6. The c2-bishop wasn't attacked, and after dxe4 the f3-rook is hit.
Material is equal, so nothing is 'won back'. The real point of exd5 is stopping dxc6, which attacks the knight.
The h3 pawn attacks the knight on g4, not a bishop. From e5, Nxe5 attacks no rook.
Nxe5 regains the pawn with tempo on the queen; in the engine line Bf6 later hits the queen on d4.
The e4-knight is not loose; d5 defends it. Still, two attackers win a pawn and remove a strong knight.
Ne7 moves the g8 knight and only defends the pinned c6 knight. It creates no threat, so there is no tempo.
cxd4 removes White's d-pawn. A later ...Be6 hits Qb3, though the engine first plays ...c5 against the bishop.
The h6 pawn attacks the knight, and f3 is safe. But retreating is passive; Nxf7 keeps equality.
Nd4 attacks no rook, and the e7 bishop stays en prise to Rf7. Nothing is saved.
Kd8 moves onto the d-file, not off it. Adjacent check can't be blocked; capturing the bishop is correct.
Capturing the g3 bishop is right, but no queen trade follows; White's queen stays active, checking on g5.
e5 is not the second rank. Saving the attacked knight actively is relevant, but Nd4 was much stronger.
Capturing the b3 knight is right, but axb3 uses up the a-pawn, so no later a-pawn break exists.
Nc3 does not attack b4, and the b4-knight is not pinned. Nc3 simply develops and covers d5/e4.
The king is already on g8; Bh7+ drives it to f8 or h8. Engine prefers Re3, and e5-capture follow-up is unexplained.
b2 isn't truly free: Black is already up material, and Qxb2 lets White take c5 with initiative, falling behind Nh6.
A knight on f5 does not attack c4. It eyes d4, e3, g3 and d6, so the stated purpose is wrong.
Bb4 doesn't block a diagonal; it pins and attacks White's c3 queen, winning it. The stated idea misreads the position.
The king already stands on g2. Qg6+ really forces Ng5 and wins material after Bd8 and hxg5.
Nf3 gains no tempo and no bishop is pinned; it blocks Bb7's attack on the h1 rook.
Nc6 doesn't attack the c3-knight, and nothing pins it. No tempo is gained; it is just development.
e8 is Black's back rank, not second rank; idea misses the real point of escaping e5xf6.
gxh4 does win a free pawn, since Nf3 guards h4. But it leaves doubled h-pawns; Nxh4 is better.
Nxe4 regains a pawn, and the engine line soon plays c4, though cxd4 first was slightly better.
Material is equal, so no bishop needs winning back. After Qa5+, White simply blocks, and the queen no longer eyes c2.
The e6 pawn isn't free; d5 attacks it. Exd5 is right because it wins back the d5 pawn and opens the centre.
Nc3 blocks no Black bishop's diagonal toward the king. It actually defends the attacked Be4 from Re8.
Bxd4 wins back the piece, and the d4 bishop defends e3 against Nf5. It is the engine's top move.
Qd3 is a queen move; no knight goes to d3. The queen guards Nc3 and eyes h7 instead.
Saving the attacked knight is correct, but g5 is not central; it is an attacking post eyeing f7 and h7.
Taking the free queen is right, but White has no knight check available; that check doesn't exist.
c5 is Black's pawn, so White cannot 'keep' it. d5 also ignores the stronger Nxb5.
After gxf3 exf3 the e4 pawn vanishes, so there's nothing to attack. gxf3 also exposes White's king to Qxh3.
e4 gains tempo on Nf3; after Ne5, Black's queen (Qd4/Qd6) hits the exposed knight, matching the engine line.
Ne5 isn't a second-rank retreat, doesn't touch f4, and f4 holds White's queen, not Black's.
Rxg2+ itself captures g2, so nothing is won back later. The real point is ...Re7, winning the f7 bishop.
Qxa2 saves the attacked queen and wins a pawn, but Black has no king attack; the queen returns to e6.
Qxb4 does save the attacked queen and wins a pawn, but no queen trade follows; White plays Rb1.
Material is level, so nothing is being won back. Nc6 does block the diagonal, but it guards b7, not an a-pawn.
The a2 rook is undefended (Be2 blocks Rf2), so Bxa2 wins it outright; this is the engine's best move.
White is not in check, and h7 offers the pawn to the king, not a rook. Qg7+ mates.
Be2 attacks neither the d8 rook nor f7, so there's no tempo. It just reopens the d-file.
Nf4 saves the knight attacked by h5 and hits h5, plus d5 and g2. This matches the engine's best move.
Qxe5 saves the queen and wins a pawn, but creates no real threat; Qc8 wins decisively.
f5 holds a knight, not a bishop. Bxf5 Bxf5 also pins Black's g6-knight to the king.
Nh6 only saves the attacked knight. Nothing forces White to give up material; Bxh6 later is White's free choice.
Rd1+ Ke7 then fxg4 works, but the check helps Black: it activates the king and guards f7.
f6 does attack the undefended g5 bishop, but it doesn't open the f-file; the pawn still blocks it.
There is no pin. Rd1 is giving check. Re1 just blocks and loses the rook to Rxe1+, while Kh2 mates.
No bishops or queens exist on the board; Rad8 gives back no rook. The idea is fictional.
Bd3 doesn't attack the b7 bishop, and it leaves the queen on d5 hanging to Bxd5.
King is already on h5; Ng7+ drives it away. Be2# mates immediately, so the check wastes it.
Check is real, but Kf8 heads toward the center; Kh8 is the safer corner square and engine-best.
The checking rook on c1 is undefended, so capturing it is correct. The queen is lost either way.
Qh5 is on the fifth rank, not the second, and doesn't attack e6. It ignores the ...Qxh2+ threat.
The b5 pawn pins nothing. cxb5 opens the c-file, so Black plays ...Qxc2 first and wins material.
No black piece defends d5, so Rxd5 wins the bishop and reaches the engine's equal line.
Nd2 blocks no bishop diagonal; the Ba3 lines are a3-f8 and a3-c1. Nd2 forks Qb3 and Rf1.
Ra6 hangs nothing; no Black piece attacks a6. Bishop e7 and queen b8 share no diagonal.
Bxf6+ Rxf6 just gives up the bishop. Without prior Kh1, Black's e3 counterplay makes the 'Qh6' plan meaningless.
Bxe7 itself captures the e7 rook, so 'win back' makes no sense. It also ignores Bxd4 winning the knight.
Rg8 saves the attacked rook and hits the g7 bishop, forcing Bd4; that matches the engine's best line.
Rf8 does attack the bishop, but nothing to do with e5. 1...e6 first traps the bishop; Rf8 lets it escape.
No black bishop is attacked, and Qd4 never touches e6. Its real point is pinning White's queen against the king.
Kd8 stays on the back rank, not the second. The c6 bishop is White's, and Bd5 soon trades it off.
Rg3+ drops the rook to Qxg3 on the d6-g3 diagonal; no king win, no a8-rook grab.
The king is already on h2, and a7 is Black's own pawn. Qe5+ actually forces a queen trade to parry mating threats.
A rook on b8 cannot attack g2. Rb8 takes the open b-file to double on the second rank.
The c6 knight is pinned on the c-file; Nxd4 allows Rxc8+ Rxc8 Rxc8+, losing a rook. It attacks no rook.
d2 is already defended by Nc4 and Rg2, and Rff2 creates no real threat. Kh8 was needed.
Rc1 recaptures, so the rook isn't free; Nxe1 wins the exchange. White's king is on g1, not central.
c5 does hit the queen and ...b4 can follow at the knight, though Qd5 hitting a8 regains time.
e6 is not Black's second rank, and a bishop on e6 cannot guard e7. Be6 also walks into Bxe6.
Rxf5 regains the pawn and attacks the h5 knight along the fifth rank. Engine slightly prefers exf5.
Recapturing the rook to restore material is correct, but a rook on c1 does not guard or attack e8.
Qf8 captures no pawn and there is no a2-bishop; the queen just hangs to Rxf8+.
Black has no c-pawn to push. Nxa1+ also leaves Rb8 hanging to Bc7; O-O first saves it.
Bh2 gives check; Kh1 walks into a discovered check from Qh3 that wins material. Kf2 limits losses.
Rg3 stays on the third rank and doesn't guard the king; the rook on f3 already protected the queen.
g3 does kick the f4-knight, but it doesn't open the g-file; the g-pawn just advances.
The king already stands on g7, and Qg3+ drives it to h8. Winning back f6 is a real follow-up.
Rc8 does not attack the a7 queen, so there is no tempo. The h-pawn push is no real plan; Rg6 is best.
Rc3 defends c6, so the knight isn't loose. bxc6 opens the b-file against Nb5, a knight, not a rook.
Bd6 is undefended and winning it is right, but Bxd6 forks neither queen nor rook; it eyes b8.
The king is already on g6 and material is equal, so there's no pawn to win back. Rg8+ only chases the king away.
Kicking and attacking g5 are the same act. f6 weakens the a2-g8 diagonal (Bd5+) and blocks Bg7.
Rxd8 does stop Rxd6 winning a pawn, but c4 is far stronger: Rxd6 exd6+ Kxd6 cxb5 wins material.
The b3 bishop isn't attacked. Still, trading on d5 and then Rc3 hitting the f3 bishop matches the engine's line.
Re6 does hit the pinned e7 bishop and threatens Rxf6; Rf8 guards f6 and parries it, near-equal to Rd8.
